claim: Persistent reservoirs remain the major obstacles to achieve an HIV-1 cure.
source: Persistent reservoirs remain the major obstacles to achieve an HIV-1 cure.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the HIV cure field.

claim: Prolonged early antiretroviral therapy (ART) may reduce the extent of reservoirs and allow for virological control after ART discontinuation.
source: Prolonged early antiretroviral therapy (ART) may reduce the extent of reservoirs and allow for virological control after ART discontinuation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential outcomes of early ART.

claim: A decade of early ART reduced the total HIV-1 DNA levels compared with later treatment initiation.
source: A decade of early ART reduced the total and integrated HIV-1 DNA levels compared with later treatment initiation, but not reaching the low levels found in LTNPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study comparing SRCV on ART and Chronic ART cohorts.

claim: A decade of early ART reduced the integrated HIV-1 DNA levels compared with later treatment initiation.
source: A decade of early ART reduced the total and integrated HIV-1 DNA levels compared with later treatment initiation, but not reaching the low levels found in LTNPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study comparing SRCV on ART and Chronic ART cohorts.

claim: Early ART does not reduce HIV-1 DNA levels to the low levels found in LTNPs.
source: A decade of early ART reduced the total and integrated HIV-1 DNA levels compared with later treatment initiation, but not reaching the low levels found in LTNPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing SRCV on ART and LTNP cohorts.

claim: Total HIV-1 DNA in rectal biopsies did not differ between cohorts.
source: Total HIV-1 DNA in rectal biopsies did not differ between cohorts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rectal biopsy measurements across cohorts.

claim: Lower viral transcription (HIV-1 unspliced RNA) was found in early compared to late-treated patients.
source: Importantly, lower viral transcription (HIV-1 unspliced RNA) and enhanced immune preservation (CD4/CD8), reminiscent of LTNPs, were found in early compared to late-treated patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing HIV-1 usRNA levels between SRCV on ART and Chronic ART cohorts.

claim: Enhanced immune preservation (CD4/CD8 ratio) was found in early compared to late-treated patients.
source: Importantly, lower viral transcription (HIV-1 unspliced RNA) and enhanced immune preservation (CD4/CD8), reminiscent of LTNPs, were found in early compared to late-treated patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CD4/CD8 ratios between SRCV on ART and Chronic ART cohorts.

claim: Early treatment is associated with some immunovirological features of LTNPs that may improve the outcome of future interventions aimed at a functional cure.
source: This suggests that early treatment is associated with some immunovirological features of LTNPs that may improve the outcome of future interventions aimed at a functional cure.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed similarities between early-treated patients and LTNPs.

claim: A reservoir of long-lived latently HIV-1 infected cells is established early in the course of the infection.
source: A reservoir of long-lived latently HIV-1 infected cells is established early in the course of the infection.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The HIV-1 reservoir persists despite suppressed viremia in patients undergoing effective antiretroviral therapy (ART).
source: It persists despite suppressed viremia in patients undergoing effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) and fuels viral rebound upon treatment discontinuation (Wong et al., 1997; Finzi et al., 1997; Chun et al., 1997; Finzi et al., 1999; Fernandez et al., 2005; Alexaki et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The HIV-1 reservoir fuels viral rebound upon treatment discontinuation.
source: It persists despite suppressed viremia in patients undergoing effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) and fuels viral rebound upon treatment discontinuation (Wong et al., 1997; Finzi et al., 1997; Chun et al., 1997; Finzi et al., 1999; Fernandez et al., 2005; Alexaki et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The HIV-1 reservoir is present in blood and tissues such as lymphoid organs, the gut and potentially the central nervous system.
source: Not only is this reservoir present in blood, but also in tissues such as lymphoid organs, the gut and potentially the central nervous system (Chun et al., 2008; Sturdevant et al., 2015; Bednar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanisms underlying HIV-1 persistence have not been fully elucidated.
source: The mechanisms underlying HIV-1 persistence have not been fully elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement of current scientific knowledge gaps.

claim: An initial decay of HIV-1 reservoirs is observed after ART intervention.
source: Although an initial decay of these reservoirs is observed after ART intervention, it is assumed that replenishment may occur through clonal proliferation of infected CD4 T cells during ART (Chomont et al., 2009; Josefsson et al., 2013; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2014) or through residual virus production despite suppressive ART (Chun et al., 2008; Buzon et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2013a) possibly in sanctuary sites where ART penetration is suboptimal (Yukl et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Replenishment of HIV-1 reservoirs may occur through clonal proliferation of infected CD4 T cells during ART.
source: Although an initial decay of these reservoirs is observed after ART intervention, it is assumed that replenishment may occur through clonal proliferation of infected CD4 T cells during ART (Chomont et al., 2009; Josefsson et al., 2013; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2014) or through residual virus production despite suppressive ART (Chun et al., 2008; Buzon et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2013a) possibly in sanctuary sites where ART penetration is suboptimal (Yukl et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Replenishment of HIV-1 reservoirs may occur through residual virus production despite suppressive ART.
source: Although an initial decay of these reservoirs is observed after ART intervention, it is assumed that replenishment may occur through clonal proliferation of infected CD4 T cells during ART (Chomont et al., 2009; Josefsson et al., 2013; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2014) or through residual virus production despite suppressive ART (Chun et al., 2008; Buzon et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2013a) possibly in sanctuary sites where ART penetration is suboptimal (Yukl et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Residual virus production may occur in sanctuary sites where ART penetration is suboptimal.
source: Although an initial decay of these reservoirs is observed after ART intervention, it is assumed that replenishment may occur through clonal proliferation of infected CD4 T cells during ART (Chomont et al., 2009; Josefsson et al., 2013; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2014) or through residual virus production despite suppressive ART (Chun et al., 2008; Buzon et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2013a) possibly in sanctuary sites where ART penetration is suboptimal (Yukl et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Low levels of viral reservoirs have been associated with an absence of viral rebound after treatment discontinuation in several case reports and the Visconti cohort.
source: Low levels of viral reservoirs have been associated with an absence of viral rebound after treatment discontinuation in several case reports and the Visconti cohort, suggesting the possibility of post-treatment virological control even in the presence of viral reservoirs (Salgado et al., 2011; Van Gulck et al., 2012; Saez-Cirion et al., 2013; Kinloch-de Loes et al., personal communication).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and case reports.

claim: Post-treatment virological control is possible even in the presence of viral reservoirs.
source: Low levels of viral reservoirs have been associated with an absence of viral rebound after treatment discontinuation in several case reports and the Visconti cohort, suggesting the possibility of post-treatment virological control even in the presence of viral reservoirs (Salgado et al., 2011; Van Gulck et al., 2012; Saez-Cirion et al., 2013; Kinloch-de Loes et al., personal communication).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited case reports and cohort studies.

claim: Long-term control of HIV-1 replication in the absence of ART is widely defined as a functional cure.
source: Achieving such a long-term control of HIV-1 replication in the absence of ART is widely defined as a functional cure (Saag and Deeks, 2010; Fauci and Folkers, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations defining the term 'functional cure'.

claim: A low saturation of viral reservoirs facilitated by early treatment initiation might be a necessary condition for post-treatment virological control, although not in itself sufficient.
source: A low saturation of viral reservoirs facilitated by early treatment initiation might be a necessary condition, although not in itself sufficient for post-treatment virological control (Saez-Cirion et al., 2013; Van Gulck et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The interplay between virological and immunological parameters is likely to be fundamental to achieve post-treatment virological control.
source: Recent evidence indicates that the interplay between virological and immunological parameters is likely to be fundamental to achieve this goal (Cellerai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Early treatment initiation with ART will likely become the standard clinical practice in HIV care.
source: Early treatment initiation with ART will likely become the standard clinical practice in HIV care.
evidence: This is a prediction based on clinical trial outcomes.

claim: The START study showed a considerably lower risk of developing AIDS and other serious conditions with early treatment initiation compared to later treatment initiation.
source: This is supported by the recent outcome of the first large-scale international 'Strategic Timing of AntiRetroviral Treatment' (START) study, showing a considerably lower risk of developing AIDS and other serious conditions when compared to later treatment initiation (INSIGHT START Study Group, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the START study.

claim: Early treatment initiation during HIV-1 seroconversion is the most effective intervention to limit the extent of viral reservoirs.
source: Interestingly, early treatment initiation during HIV-1 seroconversion is also the most effective intervention to limit the extent of viral reservoirs (Ananworanich et al., 2012; Hoen et al., 2007; Hocqueloux et al., 2013; Ananworanich et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Very low or even undetectable HIV-1 DNA has been described when treatment is initiated during the very early stages of primary HIV-1 infection (PHI).
source: Very low or even undetectable HIV-1 DNA has been described when treatment is initiated during the very early stages of primary HIV-1 infection (PHI) (Ananworanich et al., 2012; Laanani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A lower level of HIV-1 transcription has been described in ART-treated patients who initiated treatment during seroconvertion.
source: In addition, a lower level of HIV-1 transcription has been described in ART-treated patients who initiated treatment during seroconvertion (Schmid et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Elite controllers and long-term non-progressors (LTNPs) display low or undetectable blood reservoirs.
source: These HIV-1 infected individuals display low or undetectable blood reservoirs, and are able to control viremia over the long-term with limited CD4 T cell loss in the absence of treatment.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about LTNPs.

claim: Elite controllers and LTNPs are able to control viremia over the long-term with limited CD4 T cell loss in the absence of treatment.
source: These HIV-1 infected individuals display low or undetectable blood reservoirs, and are able to control viremia over the long-term with limited CD4 T cell loss in the absence of treatment.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about LTNPs.

claim: Replication-competent viruses can still be found in LTNPs despite low viral reservoirs.
source: Although their viral reservoirs have been shown to be low, replication-competent viruses can still be found in these individuals (Blankson et al., 2007; Buzon et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LTNPs display strong HIV-1-specific T cells responses with polyfunctionality.
source: LTNPs display strong HIV-1-specific T cells responses with polyfunctionality, thereby suggesting a role of T cell immunity in viremia control (Cellerai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Strong HIV-1-specific T cell responses in LTNPs suggest a role of T cell immunity in viremia control.
source: LTNPs display strong HIV-1-specific T cells responses with polyfunctionality, thereby suggesting a role of T cell immunity in viremia control (Cellerai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research about LTNP immune responses.

claim: Eighty-four patients were included in this cross-sectional study from four different cohorts.
source: Eighty-four patients were included in this cross-sectional study from four different cohorts: patients who had undergone a decade of successful ART, initiated either during seroconversion (SRCV on ART; n = 25) or during the chronic phase of the infection (Chronic ART, n = 32), LTNPs (n = 17), and recently infected ART-naïve seroconverters (Recent SRCV; n = 10) (Figure 1; Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and patient enrollment.

claim: The CD4 nadir was significantly different between each of the cohorts except between SRCV on ART and Recent SRCV.
source: The CD4 nadir was significantly different between each of the cohorts (p < 0.001) except between SRCV on ART and Recent SRCV (p = 0.623).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of patient data.

claim: All patient cohorts had detectable levels of total HIV-1 DNA in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs).
source: All patient cohorts had detectable levels of total HIV-1 DNA in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs).
